questions.q: Why do supply curves normally slope upwards?
options: Higher prices imply higher profits, giving firms an incentive to produce more
Costs always fall as output rises
questions.why: The profit incentive is the spec reason: higher price, higher profit, more output.

questions.q: Which of these would shift a supply curve to the left?
options: A new indirect tax on the good
questions.why: A tax acts like a cost of production, so less is supplied at every price.

questions.q: Which of these would shift the supply curve of smartphones to the right?
options: A rise in the price of smartphones
A fall in the cost of microchips
questions.why: Lower input costs allow more to be supplied at every price. The price change is a movement; incomes affect demand.

questions.q: A rise in a good's own price causes an extension of supply.
questions.why: Own price changes cause movements along the curve.

questions.q: Under perfect competition, the supply curve is the marginal cost curve.
questions.why: A firm supplies one more unit only if the price at least covers the cost of making it.

questions.q: A very good harvest of apples will:
questions.why: More apples are available at every price.

questions.q: Explain why a rise in the price of a good gives firms an incentive to supply more.

ideas.label: A higher price means higher profit on each unit
So firms expand production, or resources move to it

questions.model: A higher price means each unit brings in more profit, so production becomes more attractive. Firms expand output and resources move towards the good.
questions.why: Price is a signal and profit is the incentive.

tests.answer: Higher prices mean higher profits so firms want to produce more.
